claim: The lease lives in ~/.noctus/release-steward.json and is explicitly per-machine (release-steward.md rule), so the guardian-and-N-stewards design silently assumes one laptop. Cloud sessions, a second machine, or a CI-hosted steward cannot see the lease, so two guardians can coexist the moment the owner runs a cloud session. Spec point: define the guardian lease as a repo-visible/remote record (e.g. a ref or row on origin/dev or the DB) with the local file only a cache, and state explicitly that branch stewards on other machines deliver via action=request into that shared outbox.

The brief leaves 'multipliable to different environment' (P6) open, but the six-month need is almost certainly stewards per product, per machine/cloud session, and per target (dev vs prod, VPS vs future hosts). The spec should define a steward's identity as role + branch + scope declared in the role registry (branch-steward:<branch> already exists) and make the guardian's deliver/deploy contract environment-parameterised rather than hardcoded to origin/dev and the single VPS. Otherwise each new environment forks the guardian.

The guardian is a single point of failure with no supervisor (P7): a stale lease can be taken by ANY session, and with N stewards the cost of a wrong or absent guardian grows linearly. Spec point: a guardian is claimable only by a session whose role is declared guardian-eligible, a takeover must read a durable handoff record (in-flight queue entries, pending deploy asks, consent transcript location) written on every state change, and an ops-steward/watchdog flags a stale guardian to the owner.

The delivery contract is prose, but at N stewards the guardian cannot review each branch by hand (P4: it rebased a 50-commit merge-built branch and left a worktree mid-rebase). Spec point: a machine-checked 'deliverable' preflight (a release_steward action=request validation) that rejects a request unless the branch is pushed, 0-behind origin/dev via merge-built or already-rebased by the steward, own migration numbers renumbered, and CI-green locally; the guardian never rebases or edits a steward's branch and returns a REJECTED-with-reason to the steward instead. This also removes the need for the guardian to touch steward worktrees at all.

Deploy coordination does not scale to N stewards plus an owner who sleeps: consent must be typed by the owner in the session that runs the action (P5), so every steward's deploy ask competes for one human window. Spec point: stewards file deploy intents (not deploys) into a guardian-owned batch; the guardian assembles ONE deploy manifest per consent window (what shipped, migrations, rollback), the owner types consent once for the batch, and standing pre-approved classes (code-only, auto-rollback net) can run unattended while schema/exposure changes wait.

P3 versus the owner's 'ONLY queueing, merge and deploy': the guardian building steward tooling mixes roles, and the proposed 'fast lane' for tooling bugs invites every steward to demand one. Spec point: tooling owned by a dedicated tooling branch steward whose deliveries enter the same queue, with only a narrowly defined hotfix class (a bug blocking the queue itself) allowed to jump the order, recorded as such.

Where the team-of-teams 'manager' sits is unspecified and will matter at scale: cross-steward conflicts (two stewards on one file, migration numbers, shared seed changes) need a decision owner who is neither the guardian (queue/deploy only) nor either steward. Spec point: the guardian detects file/migration collisions at request time and routes them to the smallest common manager (the owner or a designated orchestrator), and tags the requests blocked-on-collision rather than choosing a winner.

P4 root cause is not a tooling bug but a boundary violation: the guardian mutated a branch steward's worktree (rebase in the owner's checkout). Spec point: the guardian NEVER runs a mutating git command in a worktree it does not own; it works only from its own scratch clone/worktree, and enqueue pushes the delivered sha as-is to mq/*. A branch that cannot be enqueued unchanged is returned to its steward, not repaired.

The delivery contract should be one mechanical predicate checked at request time, not guardian judgment: the branch head contains origin/dev (0-behind, merge-built allowed) or git merge-tree against dev is clean, keepers green, migration numbers renumbered. request refuses otherwise with the reason. The guardian then never rebases, renumbers or edits, which makes the 'rebased a merge-built branch' failure impossible by construction; merge-queue.md invariant 4 (queue never edits an entry) should be extended to the guardian.

The 'ONLY queue, merge, deploy' rule conflicts with the lease holder building steward tooling, and the proposed fast lane is inherited habit. Tooling is just another branch owned by a tooling branch steward and delivered through the same request path; urgency is a priority field on the request (guardian orders the drain), not a role exception. The guardian keeps lease, consent transcript and drain loop only, so its context stays small and replaceable.

The owner's word 'guardian' appears in no doc; the docs call the same job 'release steward', 'dev steward', 'lease holder', 'tree deployer', and the owner also calls the guardian 'the single steward that deals with all other stewards'. A newcomer cannot tell guardian = dev steward = tree deployer, nor whether 'steward' means the deployer or a branch owner. Proposed spec point: a glossary at the top of release-steward.md mapping owner word to doc word (guardian = dev steward = lease holder = tree deployer; steward = branch steward = team orchestrator) and use ONE term per role in docs, tools and hooks.

Ejection handling contradicts the owner's words: queue-lifecycle-decision has the dev steward dispatch a rescue engineer on a rescue-<slug> branch, which makes the guardian a developer of other stewards' work. Under 'stewards take branches and deliver the goal', an ejected entry returns to the branch steward with the failure log, because the branch steward is long-lived by definition and holds the context; the 'requester is done/ended' case disappears since a steward ends only after its delivery lands. The guardian only withdraws the mq ref, records the cause, and notifies the steward's ROLE.

The owner says the guardian deals 'ONLY' with queue, merge and deploy, but the existing spec gives the dev steward more: queue-lifecycle-decision has it fix ejected entries via rescue branches (dispatching rescue engineers), run prod migrations, and the current holder builds steward tooling (P3). Owner's own earlier line says stewards 'finish tasks all the way' while the steward 'fixes and never hands back', so who owns a broken delivery is contradictory. Proposed spec point: an explicit never-list for the guardian (never authors feature code or steward tooling, never edits a delivery branch) and a rule that a rejected delivery returns to its branch steward, not a rescue branch by the guardian.

'Multipliable to different environment' (P6) should not become a new role. First-principles reading: an environment is a parameter of a deploy request (target=dev|prod|product-slug), not a kind of steward; N stewards across N environments all use the same request, and the guardian serializes per target with one lock. Do not design multi-guardian or per-environment guardians until a second machine or cloud session actually needs one; ask the owner this single question rather than speculating.

release-steward.md is titled and numbered as 'ONE session handles CI and deploy; everyone else files requests' (sections 1-7), while the multi-steward model (branch stewards, roles, dev vs branch steward) is bolted on in section 8 under 'Reboot' with a dangling line 'topology under review (council f93e1991): shape C' pointing at a decision file on another branch. A reader of sections 1-7 would not know branch stewards exist, and an owner re-reading it would not recognise the model they described. Proposed: promote branch steward to a first-class section (roles, boundaries, delivery contract) and remove or resolve the 'under review' placeholder once this council is ratified.

Deploy coordination: the owner's consent cannot be delegated, so the guardian is a consent-holder, not a decider. Spec: a steward's request carries deploy=true plus target and sha pin; the guardian merges to dev without consent but parks deploy requests as pending_consent, lists them in one owner-facing summary, and executes only when the owner types consent in the guardian's own session. Owner asleep means dev merges proceed and prod deploys wait; no relayed consent, no auto-deploy.

The owner's phrase 'stewards are multipliable to different environment' is unexplained and the docs never define 'environment' (dev fleet is dormant, prod is the only live one; branch steward is per BRANCH, not per environment). Guessing wrongly would build the wrong scaling model (per product? per machine? per cloud session?). Proposed: do not write the spec for this sentence until the owner answers one multiple-choice question (product / dev-vs-prod / another machine or cloud session), and until then specify the guardian as one lease per machine with the multi-machine case marked explicitly out of scope.

Guardian supervision (P7) does not need a supervisor if the guardian is stateless: all state lives in the lease, inbox and outbox files, so a dead guardian is replaced by any leader session via claim and resumes by reading them. Concerning the stale-lease takeover risk, require claim to print the pending inbox and the in-flight mq refs and to refuse while a CI run it owns is in flight unless the TTL passed. In the team-of-teams tree the guardian is a service leaf under the root manager, never a manager; proposals about its process go up to that manager.

The 'manager' of team-of-teams and the owner's 'guardian' look like the same thing to a newcomer but are different: the manager decides disputes (for cross-team ones it is the owner), the guardian only executes queue and deploy. The owner says stewards 'coordinate deploy with the guardian' and the guardian 'deals with' all stewards, which reads as supervision, yet no doc says the guardian can arbitrate or reorder deliveries. Proposed spec point: state in one sentence that the guardian is a service peer, not a manager; disputes between stewards go to the owner (or a declared manager), and the guardian orders deliveries only by a stated rule (FIFO by request, with an owner-set priority override).

The same role carries three names in the docs (release steward, dev steward, guardian), and merge-queue.md section 4 still says the owning session fixes ejections while queue-lifecycle-decision says the steward fixes. Inherited naming habit causes the confusion the owner reports; pick one name (guardian) and one ejection rule, and update both docs in the same change. Two stewards touching one file need no special role: the guardian serializes landings and the later steward merges dev again, which the 0-behind predicate already forces.

The delivery contract is nowhere written as a checklist; the brief itself uses unexplained jargon ('merge-built vs rebased', 'train', '0-behind', 'riders', 'uncertain', 'ejected'), and P4 shows the cost: the guardian rebased a merge-built 50-commit branch and left someone else's worktree mid-rebase. Proposed spec: a one-page delivery contract the branch steward self-checks before action=request (pushed, 0 commits behind origin/dev, merged not rebased, tests green on the merged tree, migration numbers renumbered, derived artifacts regenerated); the guardian refuses non-conforming requests with the failing item named and NEVER mutates a branch or any other session's worktree.

Deploy coordination leaves the owner-asleep case unnamed: consent must be typed by the owner in the session that runs the action (P5), so with N stewards asking, the owner must know that only the guardian session receives the consent and which deliveries it covers. Also P7 (who watches or replaces a stale guardian; today any session may claim a stale lease) is unresolved and sounds alarming to a newcomer. Proposed: a plain-words 'deploy request' record that lists what will ship, the guardian shows it to the owner as one consent ask, and a stale-lease takeover must announce itself and re-read the pending consents rather than inherit them.

The lease (~/.noctus/release-steward.json, release-steward.md spec 1) is per machine, so 'ONE guardian no matter how many stewards' is only true on one laptop; cloud sessions, other machines or another 'environment' (P6) each elect their own guardian and race on origin/dev and the one VPS. Spec point: the single-guardian lock must live at a shared authority (e.g. a lease ref or file on origin, checked before enqueue and deploy), with the local file only as cache; otherwise the owner's invariant is unenforced exactly where 'multipliable' stewards are added.

The guardian's enqueue path rebased a 50-commit merge-built branch IN THE BRANCH STEWARD'S WORKTREE and left it mid-rebase (P4); the contradiction is that the guardian was allowed to mutate a branch it does not own, then was denied the repair. Spec point: the guardian NEVER writes to a steward's worktree or branch; it composes only in its own scratch worktree from the pushed ref, any non-atomic compose failure leaves the source untouched, and merge-built branches are merged (never rebased, merge-queue.md already says --no-ff trains are merged) -- make the rebase of a branch containing merge commits a refusal, not a path.

A delivery contract of 'pushed 0-behind dev' is unsatisfiable under contention: dev advances every CI cycle (~25 min), so N stewards chase the tip forever (livelock) and the guardian is blamed for what is a moving target. Spec point: the contract is 'merge-built (dev merged INTO the branch, never rebased), pushed, git merge-tree against current origin/dev reports no conflict, local scoped checks green, migration number and derived files pre-resolved'; the queue composes the rest, and on a conflict ejection the branch steward re-merges dev and re-requests.

The owner says the guardian deals ONLY with queue/merge/deploy, but queue-lifecycle-decision.md (b5's requirement 2 and 'steward fixes the ejected entry itself via a rescue branch') and P3 (lease holder builds steward tooling) make the guardian also a fixer and toolsmith, so the 'ONLY' boundary is already contradicted by docs and practice. Spec point: ejection fixes belong to the branch steward that owns the content (the guardian reports the cause and the exact conflict); tooling bugs found by the guardian are filed as proposals to the tooling steward's team and land through the same queue, with one named emergency exception (a one-commit fix on a rescue branch, logged) rather than a standing 'fast lane'.

The strongest case for the option not chosen: the guardian is a human-in-the-loop session sitting on the MERGE path, which makes it the single point of failure for landings (P4 stuck until the owner wakes) when the queue is already an automated, serialising CI mechanism. Alternative spec: stewards enqueue their own conflict-safe deliveries (the 'open enqueue' item 1 of the queue-lifecycle spec), and the guardian is narrowed to what truly needs a single serial actor with owner consent: prod promote, migrations ordering, deploy, plus queue health watching. This keeps the owner's 'one tree deployer' while removing the merge SPOF.

Prod consent must be typed by the owner in the session that runs the action (P5), so with N stewards and the owner asleep every deploy request queues behind one consent and nothing scales past the owner's waking hours; the brief's 'coordinate deploy with the guardian' has no mechanism for that. Spec point: stewards file deploy requests with a readiness manifest (sha, migrations, rollback plan, predeploy_check result); the guardian batches them into ONE consent prompt per window, and consent riders (ship-consent-riders.md) carry an explicit scope and expiry so a pre-typed rider can cover a named, bounded batch while the owner sleeps; absent a valid rider, the guardian lands to dev and holds prod.

Stale-guardian takeover (any session may claim a stale lease, spec 9) can create two deployers: a guardian that is merely slow mid-deploy or mid-migration is replaced, and the new holder starts a second image swap. Spec point: the guardian writes an in-flight action journal (action, sha, step, started_at) next to the lease; a takeover must first read it, may only resume or roll back that action, and is refused while the old pid is alive or the journal is open; a watchdog (ops-steward or the owner notification) alerts on a stale lease, and no agent supervises the guardian beyond that -- escalation goes to the owner per team-of-teams.

Two stewards touching one file are discovered only at ejection (about 25 minutes lost, then a fix by whoever), and team-of-teams routes cross-team disputes to the owner, who is asleep. Spec point: each request declares its touched paths/collision class at filing time; the guardian serialises overlapping requests in one train or orders them (first filed wins), tells the later steward before enqueue, and the two steward orchestrators exchange position reports through the guardian's inbox rather than waiting for the owner.

The owner's wording makes the guardian look like the 'manager of all stewards', while team-of-teams.md says the guardian is a peer deployer and the manager of different teams is the owner, so decisions that cross teams would flow to the guardian or to a sleeping owner. Spec point: define the guardian's authority as over the LANE only (order, hold, refuse unfit deliveries, deploy timing) and none over content or priorities; disputes about content go to the owner; write this in one role table in release-steward.md section 8 and remove 'dev steward' / 'branch steward' naming drift.

P6 and P7 are unresolved owner-intent ambiguities that change the architecture (environment = product, dev/prod, machine, or cloud session; supervised guardian or not); designing before the owner answers risks the same confusion the owner flagged. Spec point: ask the owner two bounded questions via noc-questionnaire (what 'environment' means, and whether a watchdog alert to the owner suffices for the guardian) and ship the lane-only parts of the spec that are valid under every answer first.

task_branch enqueue mutates the requester's worktree: it runs on the branch steward's wt_path, and for any branch carrying a merge commit it first MERGES origin/dev into it (task_branch.py ~3080 _train.sync_with_dev, committing onto their branch) then runs git rebase --rebase-merges; on conflict it only aborts if a rebase-merge/rebase-apply dir exists (_rebase_in_progress), so a failed sync-merge or a mid-state leaves the owner's worktree half-edited, exactly P4. Proposed spec: the guardian NEVER rebases or merges a delivery. Contract is 'pushed, 0 behind origin/dev, merge-built or linear, all gates green'; the guardian's enqueue must be a pure push of that sha to mq/<slug>--<sha7> in a throwaway worktree or via 'git push remote <sha>:refs/heads/mq/...' with no checkout of the steward's tree, and a delivery that is behind dev is REJECTED back to the branch steward (status=needs_resync) rather than fixed.

No machine-checked delivery contract exists: release_steward request (release_steward.py:530) accepts slug/branch/head_sha/products/migrations/notes with zero validation of behind-count, gates, mergeability or that the branch was pushed, and the guardian discovers a bad delivery only mid-enqueue. Proposed spec: 'request' runs a read-only preflight and records a verdict, refusing (status=rejected_contract) unless head is pushed to origin, merge-base == origin/dev tip (0 behind) or the behind-commits are already merge-resolved, keepers/pytest scope green, migration numbers free (next_migration_number), and the working tree of the head is clean; the same preflight is what the guardian re-runs, so one function, two ends.

Nothing enforces 'branch stewards never enqueue/deploy/touch mq': the hook (decide_call, release_steward.py:1023) only compares session id to the lease and any session can bypass with NOC_STEWARD_OVERRIDE=<10 chars> which is self-typed and self-audited, and 'branch-steward:<branch>' is a self-set role with no capability attached. Owner asleep means an agent stuck on a refusal has a one-line escape and a stale lease any leader may claim. Proposed spec: guardian-only actions require the lease AND a role 'guardian' that only the owner-typed claim can set; override is disabled unless the owner's transcript carries a typed phrase (same verification as prod consent), and the branch-steward role records a hard deny-list in the hook.

Stale-guardian takeover is unsafe overnight: claim succeeds for ANY session when state==stale (release_steward.py:391), staleness is 7200s without heartbeat or dead pid, and a heartbeat is only refreshed by steward actions; a branch steward with shipping work will auto-claim and become guardian mid-queue with no check on in-flight mq/ entries, pending deploy, or the previous holder's unfinished tail (landed/cleanup). P7 is real. Proposed spec: takeover is allowed only after the new holder runs 'reconcile' and a mandatory takeover checklist (list mq/* refs and open queue entries, in-flight deploy marker, outbox items in state enqueued-not-acked), records them as inherited, and a deploy-in-flight marker blocks takeover until its watchdog verdict; also a two-tier TTL (short for enqueue lane, owner-only for deploy lane).

Deploy coordination is not a first-class object: the outbox request has no deploy intent, target environment, product list ordering, rollback sha, or consent reference, so 'stewards coordinate deploy with the guardian' is only free-text notes. With N stewards, two requests with migrations plus an image swap cannot be sequenced by tool, and consent typed in the guardian's session cannot be tied to a specific request. Proposed spec: add request field deploy={env,products,needs_migration,rollback_sha,verify_cmd}; the guardian builds ONE deploy plan per window from the batch, records plan hash, and prod consent (prod_consent) must quote that plan hash so a consent applies to exactly one plan; unattended runs execute only dev-fleet-dormant-safe steps and park the prod step as 'awaiting_owner' with a queued reminder.

Ejection and rollback ownership are underspecified: task_branch landed returns status=ejected telling the caller to 'fix it on the branch', but the guardian must not edit branches and the branch steward may be offline or reached only by SendMessage (best-effort, release-steward.md spec 8). Nothing records ejection back into the outbox with a retry budget, nothing quarantines a repeatedly ejected delivery so it stops blocking riders, and nothing says who reverts a landed-but-bad commit on dev. Proposed spec: eject writes outbox event ejected{reason,url}, auto-requeues the other riders without that slug, caps retries at 2, then parks it as blocked_on_owner_steward; rollback of a bad landing is a guardian-owned revert PR through the same queue, never a force-push.

Guardian vs tooling-author conflict (P3) is untestable as written: 'the guardian deals ONLY with queue, merge and deploy' conflicts with the fact that the same lease holder fixes release_steward.py and task_branch.py, and the steward tooling fast-lane request is itself delivered through the tool being fixed. Proposed spec: tooling for the lane is owned by a branch steward (tooling), delivered through the normal queue; for a bug that blocks landings the guardian may only apply a pre-approved, enumerated emergency lane (revert of the last tool commit, or NOC_STEWARD_OVERRIDE with owner-typed phrase) and must file the fix as a request, never hand-edit mid-shift; add a keeper that fails a commit touching release_steward.py/task_branch.py when the author session holds the lease.

Two stewards on one file and the 'team-of-teams manager' have no tool: request() dedups only by slug, there is no collision-class check across pending requests (files/migrations/product overlap), and an unlanded request carries no priority or order so the drain order is arbitrary. Proposed spec: inbox computes pairwise file-overlap between pending heads (git diff --name-only against merge-base) and groups overlapping ones into a train or serialises them with the earlier one first, and surfaces unresolved overlap to the manager role (the orchestrator of the smallest team containing both) via a 'collision' event instead of the guardian picking a winner.

P6 'multipliable to different environment' is unverified and the spec should not guess: current tools support exactly one lease per machine at ~/.noctus/release-steward.json, so multi-machine or multi-environment guardians are impossible without a shared lease store. Proposed spec: ask the owner one question (product, dev/prod, or machine?) before design; until answered, state in the spec that exactly ONE guardian per machine is supported and environments are a field on the request (env=dev|prod), not additional guardians.

decision: Guardian = single lane holder (queue, merge to dev, deploy) as a service leaf under the owner; branch stewards own branches end to end and deliver via one read-only deliverable(branch) preflight; enqueue becomes a pure push (no checkout, no rebase); deploy plan hash in prod consent; durable journal + takeover checklist; lease to origin before multi-machine.
biggest_risk: The 'guardian never touches another worktree' rule is prose over a tool whose enqueue merges and rebases in the requester worktree, and the fix must land through that same path; until pure-push enqueue merges, a merge-built delivery can recreate the stuck-rebase P4.
first_step: Tooling branch steward builds the read-only deliverable preflight plus pure-push enqueue in task_branch.py with real-git tests on merge-built branches, delivered linear; until it lands the guardian refuses merge-built deliveries that need a rebase.
